The value a digit has because of where it sits in a number.
In 352, the 5 is worth 50 because it is in the tens place.
Changing a number to a simpler one that is close to it, such as the nearest 10 or 100.
A place after the decimal point. The first is tenths, the second is hundredths.
A number less than zero. It has a minus sign in front.
A straight line with numbers marked in order. Numbers get bigger as you go right.
−3 is to the left of 2 on a number line.
A whole number. It can be positive, negative or zero, but not a fraction.
Part of a whole, written as one number over another.
3/4 means 3 parts out of 4 equal parts.
The top number of a fraction. It tells you how many parts you have.
The bottom number of a fraction. It tells you how many equal parts the whole is split into.
Fractions that look different but are worth the same.
A number out of 100. Per cent means “out of a hundred”.
25% is 25 out of 100, the same as 1/4.
A number that divides into another number exactly, with nothing left over.
A number in another number's times table.
A whole number with exactly two factors: 1 and itself. 1 is not prime.
What you get when you multiply a whole number by itself.
A small raised number that tells you how many times to multiply a number by itself.
A letter that stands for a number we don't know yet or that can change.
In 3x + 2, the letter x is the variable.
A group of numbers, letters and signs with no equals sign.
Putting a number in place of a letter to work out the value.
Terms with exactly the same letters, which can be added or subtracted.
A statement that two things are equal. It always has an equals sign.
Find the value of the letter that makes an equation true.
The operation that undoes another one. Adding undoes subtracting; multiplying undoes dividing.
A list of numbers that follows a rule.
One of the numbers in a sequence.
A rule that gives any term from its position n.
A pair of numbers (x, y) that gives the position of a point on a grid. Go along first, then up or down.
One of the two number lines on a graph. The x-axis goes across and the y-axis goes up.
The axes meet at the origin.
The point (0, 0), where the x-axis and y-axis cross.
Every point is measured from the origin.
How steep a straight line is: how far it goes up for each 1 it goes across.
A way to compare amounts, written with a colon.
2 : 3 means for every 2 of one thing there are 3 of the other.
When two amounts change in the same way, so if one doubles the other doubles too.
Make a ratio or fraction use the smallest whole numbers possible by dividing by a common factor.
The amount of turn between two lines that meet at a point, measured in degrees (°).
An angle of exactly 90°, like the corner of a square.
A square has four right angles.
An angle more than 90° but less than 180°.
A flat shape with straight sides that join up.
Triangles, squares and hexagons are polygons.
The total distance all the way around the edge of a shape.
A 3 cm by 5 cm rectangle has perimeter 16 cm.
How much flat space a shape covers, measured in square units such as cm².
A 3 cm by 5 cm rectangle has area 15 cm².
How much space a 3D shape takes up, measured in cubic units such as cm³.
A cube with 2 cm sides has volume 8 cm³.
Flipping a shape over a mirror line. Each point ends up the same distance from the line on the other side.
A reflection in the y-axis swaps left and right.
Turning a shape about a fixed point, by an angle and in a direction.
Sliding a shape without turning or flipping it.
Move 3 squares right and 2 squares up.
Making a shape bigger or smaller by a scale factor, keeping its shape.
Scale factor 2 makes every side twice as long.
How likely something is to happen, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).
The probability of heads on a fair coin is 1/2.
One possible result of an experiment.
Rolling a dice has 6 possible outcomes.
When every outcome is equally likely.
A fair dice lands on each number equally often in the long run.
An average: add up all the values, then divide by how many there are.
The middle value when the values are put in order.
The value that appears most often.
The biggest value take away the smallest. It shows how spread out the data is.
A push or a pull. It is measured in newtons (N).
Kicking a ball puts a force on it.
The force of gravity pulling an object down. On Earth, weight in N ≈ mass in kg × 10.
A 50 kg person weighs about 500 N on Earth.
How much matter (stuff) is in an object, measured in kilograms (kg). It is the same everywhere.
Your mass is the same on the Moon, but your weight is less.
A force that acts against movement when two surfaces rub together.
Friction slows down a sledge on the snow.
Forces that are equal in size and act in opposite directions. Nothing speeds up, slows down or changes direction.
A book resting on a table.
How far something travels in a certain time. Speed = distance ÷ time.
A car that goes 100 m in 5 s has a speed of 20 m/s.
A graph of how far something has gone over time. A steeper line means faster.
A flat line means the object is not moving.
Speeding up. (Scientists also call slowing down a kind of acceleration.)
A car pulling away from traffic lights is accelerating.
How spread out a force is. Pressure = force ÷ area.
Snowshoes spread your weight, so you sink less.
The turning effect of a force. Moment = force × distance from the pivot.
A longer spanner makes it easier to turn a nut.
The middle of a seesaw is its pivot.
What is needed to make things happen. It is measured in joules (J) and is never used up, only moved between stores.
Food has energy in a chemical store.
A way energy is held, such as kinetic, thermal, chemical, gravitational or elastic.
A stretched spring has energy in its elastic store.
Energy something has because it is moving.
A faster bike has more kinetic energy.
Energy cannot be made or destroyed, only moved from one store to another.
A falling ball moves energy from its gravitational store to its kinetic store.
How fast energy is moved. It is measured in watts (W). 1 W = 1 joule every second.
A 60 W bulb moves 60 J of energy each second.
The unit on energy bills: the energy a 1 kW appliance uses in 1 hour.
A 2 kW heater on for 3 hours uses 6 kWh.
An energy resource that will not run out, such as wind, solar or hydroelectric.
Coal is not renewable; sunlight is.
Moving quickly backwards and forwards. All sounds are made by vibrations.
A guitar string vibrates to make a note.
How many waves pass each second, measured in hertz (Hz). Higher frequency sounds have a higher pitch.
Humans can hear about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
How big a wave's vibrations are. A bigger amplitude sound is louder.
Shouting makes waves with a bigger amplitude than whispering.
A sound that bounces back off a surface.
Shout in a big empty hall and you may hear an echo.
Light bouncing off a surface. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
You see yourself in a mirror because light reflects.
Light bending when it goes from one material into another, such as air into water.
A straw looks bent in a glass of water.
The band of colours white light splits into: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
A prism or raindrops make a spectrum.
A material that light cannot pass through.
Wood is opaque, so it makes a shadow.
The flow of electric charge around a circuit, measured in amps (A).
The push that makes current flow, measured in volts (V).
A 1.5 V cell is a common battery.
How much a component slows down the current, measured in ohms (Ω).
A long thin wire has more resistance.
A circuit with only one loop, so the same current goes through every component.
If one bulb breaks, the others go out.
A circuit with more than one loop (branch).
Lights in a house are in parallel, so each can be switched on its own.
A material that lets electricity flow through it easily.
Copper and other metals are good conductors.
A material that does not let electricity flow through it easily.
Plastic covers wires because it is an insulator.
Electric charge that builds up on the surface of an object, often by rubbing.
Rub a balloon on your hair and it sticks to the wall.
A tiny particle with a negative charge. Electrons move when things are rubbed together.
An object that gains electrons becomes negatively charged.
Opposite charges pull together (attract); like charges push apart (repel).
Two negatively charged balloons push apart.
The space around a magnet where it pushes or pulls on magnetic materials.
Iron filings show the shape of a magnetic field.
A material that a magnet attracts: iron, steel, nickel and cobalt.
A paper clip made of steel sticks to a magnet.
A coil of wire that becomes a magnet when current flows through it. It can be switched off.
Scrapyard cranes use electromagnets to lift cars.
A tiny piece that all matter is made of, far too small to see.
In a solid, particles are packed close in a regular pattern.
The three main forms matter can be in: solid, liquid and gas.
Ice, water and steam are the same substance in three states.
How much mass is packed into a certain volume. Density = mass ÷ volume.
An object floats in water if it is less dense than water.
Particles spreading out from where there are lots of them to where there are fewer.
The smell of toast spreads across the kitchen.
The curved path of one object around another, held by gravity.
A force of attraction between all objects with mass.
Gravity keeps the planets orbiting the Sun.
The distance light travels in one year. It measures distance, not time.
The nearest star after the Sun is about 4 light years away.
A part of the year with its own weather. Seasons happen because the Earth's axis is tilted.
When the northern half tilts towards the Sun, it is summer there.
